query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding 0.1 at.% boron to an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy induces the precipitation of (Hf, Zr)B2 borides at grain boundaries, which in turn enhances grain-boundary cohesion and alters dislocation dynamics. This microstructural modification is expected to increase yield strength and ductility and to modify the thermoelastic response at high temperatures compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: An equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy produced with identical processing conditions (e.g., casting, homogenization) to ensure a homogeneous BCC solid-solution matrix.
generation.conditions: High-temperature tensile and nanoindentation tests conducted in the range of 700 K to 1273 K, with all alloys processed identically except for the boron addition.
generation.structural_mediator: Intergranular precipitation of (Hf, Zr)B2 borides at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The boride precipitates enhance the cohesion of grain boundaries and act as dislocation pinning sites. This modification improves the work hardenability and ductility by shifting the failure mode from primarily intergranular fracture toward a mixed (or transgranular) fracture, and it alters the thermoelastic modulus due to the modified thermal strain accommodation at the boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline undoped alloy, the boron-modified alloy will display higher yield strength, improved ductility, and altered thermoelastic modulus measured under high-temperature conditions. Additionally, microstructural analysis should reveal uniform intergranular (Hf, Zr)B2 precipitates.
generation.baseline: The same HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy without the addition of boron.
generation.boundary: The effects are expected to be significant under high-temperature conditions (700 K to 1273 K) with identical processing histories; any deviations in precipitate distribution or excessive coarsening may affect the expected behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of the improvements in mechanical properties and thermoelastic response remains uncertain, as results will depend on the uniformity and stability of the boride precipitates. Variations in processing or precipitate evolution with prolonged high-temperature exposure could also modify the outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys: one set with 0.1 at.% boron addition and one set without boron. Ensure both sets follow the exact same processing route. Conduct high-temperature tensile tests and nanoindentation experiments from 700 K to 1273 K. Perform microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, SEM, and energy-dispersive spectroscopy) to identify the presence, distribution, and uniformity of (Hf, Zr)B2 boride precipitates at grain boundaries.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-modified alloy fails to show statistically significant improvements in yield strength, ductility, or thermoelastic modulus compared to the baseline, or if the expected intergranular (Hf, Zr)B2 boride precipitation is absent or non-uniform, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion, the work hardenability and ductility were effectively improved with the addition of boron.Keywords: refractory alloy, high-entropy alloy, boride, grain boundary, mechanical prop

Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.

An equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA was developed in this study, and the addition of a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%, RHEA-B) further overcame the grain-boundary brittleness. As indicated by the microstructural observations and chemical analyses, a simple BCC-phase, solid-solution structure was formed in the matrices of both the alloys. The addition of boron did not obviously increase the hardness of the matrix but induced the intergranular precipitation of the HCP-phase (Hf, Zr)B2 borides which markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Attributable to the lattice distortions caused by the random distribution of different constituent elements, a diminished anisotropy in the mechanical properties was noticed, and the deformation behavior was mediated by many small slips on multiple {110} planes. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion with the addition of boron and the intergranular precipitation of borides, the work hardenability and ductility of the alloy were effectively improved, and the failure mode obviously changed from a mainly intergranular facture to a major portion of the transgranular fracture.

proposals.intervention: Add a minor amount (0.1 at.%) of boron to induce intergranular boride precipitation
proposals.conditions: High-temperature tensile and nanoindentation tests conducted from 700 K to 1273 K; identical processing history except for B-addition
proposals.structural_mediator: Precipitation of (Hf,Zr)B2 borides at grain boundaries
proposals.mechanism: The boride precipitates enhance grain-boundary cohesion and modify the local dislocation dynamics, thereby affecting both the mechanical strength (via dislocation pinning) and thermoelastic response (by altering thermal strain accommodation) in high-temperature conditions
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy (without boron), the B-modified alloy should exhibit higher yield strength and ductility at high temperatures along with altered thermoelastic modulus values; failure of these differences (i.e. similar properties) would falsify the hypothesis
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It proposes that boundary defect modification via a controlled second-phase (boride) formation governs the mechanical and thermoelastic behavior, providing a testable, controlled comparison with and without the intervention

proposals.intervention: Apply two distinct thermal treatments to generate different dislocation structures and short-range ordering
proposals.conditions: Subject samples to a high-temperature anneal (to minimize dislocations and promote ordering) versus a cold-rolled + low-temperature anneal state; testing at temperatures between 673 K and 873 K under identical strain rate conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Variation in dislocation density and short-range ordering in the BCC matrix
proposals.mechanism: Thermally activated rearrangements alter the dislocation core energy and mobility; the thermal treatment modulates the balance between dislocation slip and grain-boundary mediated deformation, thereby governing the alloy’s mechanical performance and elastic response at high temperature
proposals.predicted_outcome: The thermally annealed (ordered, low dislocation density) sample should show a more pronounced thermoelastic response and different yield behavior compared to the cold-worked sample; if no measurable differences occur, the hypothesis would be falsified
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It offers a controlled comparison where the effect of internal microstructural rearrangements (dislocations and ordering) on high-temperature performance is isolated, explaining changes in thermoelastic and mechanical behavior

proposals.intervention: Induce controlled near-surface dynamic amorphization through high-temperature, high-strain deformation under ultra-high vacuum versus ambient conditions
proposals.conditions: Conduct friction and wear tests in ultra-high vacuum and in controlled oxygen partial pressures while measuring in-situ temperature and deformation using nanoindentation and TEM for near-surface analysis (testing at >1273 K)
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra-nano crystalline or amorphous near-surface layer due to dynamic shear and thermal energy input
proposals.mechanism: Under high-temperature, high-strain conditions, a dynamic transformation (amorphization or nanostructuring) may occur that lowers friction and alters crack propagation, thereby modifying the alloy's thermoelastic behavior; differences in testing environments (vacuum vs oxygen) control oxidation effects
proposals.predicted_outcome: A pronounced, stress-induced amorphous layer should form in ultra-high vacuum tests, correlating with lower friction coefficients and distinct elastic moduli compared to baseline tests in ambient conditions; absence of structural change or property variation would falsify the mechanism
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It provides a mechanistic hypothesis linking in-situ microstructural evolution (dynamic amorphization) under controlled environmental and loading conditions to the observed mechanical and thermoelastic properties

proposals.intervention: Employ molecular dynamics (MD) simulations guided by the Maximum Entropy Production Rate (MEPR) approach to predict and then experimentally validate defect self-organization under different strain rates
proposals.conditions: Simulate and then test samples under controlled high-temperature (673–873 K) tensile loading at varied strain rates (0.001 to 0.0005 s⁻¹); perform corresponding high-temperature mechanical tests and in-situ TEM observations
proposals.structural_mediator: Spatial and temporal evolution of defect clusters and local chemical inhomogeneities as revealed by changes in entropy generation rates
proposals.mechanism: The MEPR principle predicts that different imposed strain rates lead to distinct self-organized defect patterns (e.g., clustering versus homogeneous distribution) that govern both thermoelasticity and dislocation-mediated plasticity in the alloy
proposals.predicted_outcome: A controlled variation in strain rate should result in a measurable difference in defect organization and associated mechanical/thermoelastic responses relative to a baseline condition; lack of such correlation would serve to falsify the hypothesis
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By coupling MD simulations with high-temperature testing, this strategy directly tests whether the self-organization of defects (quantified via entropy production) is the governing mechanism behind the alloys’ behavior, offering a clear, falsifiable prediction

critiques.addresses_problem: The hypothesis directly links high-temperature, high-strain conditions with a dynamic microstructural transformation (amorphization or nanostructuring) that would modify both friction behavior and thermoelastic properties, addressing the question’s core mechanistic uncertainty.
critiques.constraints: It respects the specified refractory alloy (WMoTaNbV), operating temperatures (>1273 K), and the requirement to compare ultra‐high vacuum versus controlled oxygen atmospheres.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically plausible; dynamic shear-induced amorphization has been previously observed (e.g., PMC7311485) and is known to affect shear strength and wear behavior.
critiques.feasibility: The experimental plan (friction tests, nanoindentation, and TEM for near-surface analysis) is feasible with established high-temperature tribological and microscopy methods.
critiques.evidence: The supporting records (PMC7311485) demonstrate dynamic amorphization in HEAs under similar conditions, providing solid support for the proposed mechanism.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that the near‐surface dynamic amorphization may predominantly affect surface tribological behavior without fully correlating with the bulk thermoelastic response.
critiques.fix: Include additional bulk characterization techniques to directly link the near-surface amorphization with changes in overall thermoelastic properties.

critiques.addresses_problem: This approach targets a mechanistic change—grain-boundary cohesion via intergranular boride precipitation—that can explain modifications in mechanical strength and thermoelastic response under high-temperature conditions.
critiques.constraints: The proposal is specific to the HfMoNbTaTiZr system, adheres to high-temperature tensile and nanoindentation testing between 700 K and 1273 K, and compares identical processing histories aside from the boron addition.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism of enhancing boundary cohesion through a second-phase (boride) formation with even 0.1 at.% boron is physically sound and has solid precedence in alloy design.
critiques.feasibility: The controlled addition of boron and subsequent microstructural and mechanical tests are well within the scope of current experimental metallurgy.
critiques.evidence: The evidence provided (PMC9572892) supports that minor boron additions lead to intergranular precipitation and enhance ductility and work hardenability.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is precise control of the boride precipitation; if the precipitates are not uniformly distributed or if they coarsen, the intended mechanical and thermoelastic benefits might not materialize.
critiques.fix: Implement more rigorous control over boron distribution and precipitate size through tailored processing parameters to ensure consistent intergranular precipitation.

critiques.addresses_problem: The strategy connects defect self-organization—predicted via the Maximum Entropy Production Rate (MEPR) principle—with variations in mechanical and thermoelastic properties, directly aiming to test the governing cause through controlled strain-rate variation.
critiques.constraints: It is applied to the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 system under high-temperature tensile conditions (673–873 K) with varied strain rates, meeting the operating constraints albeit at a slightly lower temperature range than some other directions.
critiques.physical_soundness: While the MEPR-based defect self-organization concept is theoretically intriguing and has some supporting evidence, its application to defect evolution in refractory HEAs remains less established and more exploratory.
critiques.feasibility: The combination of MD simulations with experimental tensile tests and in-situ TEM is methodologically feasible though challenging, particularly in bridging simulation time scales with experimental observations.
critiques.evidence: The references (PMC10453588, PMC8392280) discuss defect behavior and MEPR concepts, supporting the theoretical underpinnings of the approach.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk lies in the potential disconnect between MD simulation predictions (which operate on short time scales and small system sizes) and experimentally observable defect patterns at high temperatures.
critiques.fix: Complement the MD simulations with extended-time experimental studies or mesoscale modeling to better validate the predicted defect self-organization over practical time scales.

critiques.addresses_problem: This hypothesis addresses the question by investigating how thermally tuned dislocation structures and short-range ordering affect thermoelastic and mechanical behavior, thus isolating the influence of microstructural rearrangements.
critiques.constraints: The approach is tailored for the TiZrHfNbTa system and involves controlled thermal treatments with subsequent testing in the designated high-temperature range (673–873 K), conforming to the specified service conditions.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically plausible since thermal treatments are known to modify dislocation densities and ordering, which can, in turn, influence plasticity and elastic response.
critiques.feasibility: The two distinct thermal treatments (high-temperature anneal versus cold-rolling followed by low-temperature anneal) are well-established methods in materials processing, making the approach experimentally feasible.
critiques.evidence: The overall approach is consistent with previous studies on dislocation mediated plasticity in RHEAs (e.g., PMC10894205 and related records), providing a sound basis for the hypothesis.
critiques.main_risk: The key risk is that the differences induced by the thermal treatments might not be sufficiently isolated, making it challenging to conclusively link the observed thermoelastic behavior solely to changes in dislocation density and short-range order.
critiques.fix: Incorporate quantitative microstructural characterization (e.g., advanced diffraction or high-resolution TEM analysis) to precisely correlate the variations in dislocation structure with changes in mechanical and thermoelastic properties.
